//: THE SHARED IR FIXTURE SET -- read by both languages, asserted by both.
`backend/tests/test_ir_validate.py` runs every case through
`app.ir.validate`; `frontend/src/ir/fixtures.test.ts` runs the same
cases through `frontend/src/ir/validate.ts`. Neither asserts the
other's output: both assert the `code` and `loc` written down here,
which were derived by hand from `docs/contracts/problem-ir.md` and
from `backend/app/ir/contract.json`'s `rules` list. Two
implementations that agree with each other and disagree with the
contract would prove nothing.
EVERY INVALID CASE IS WRONG IN EXACTLY ONE WAY. Where a structural
fault makes a downstream rule unavoidably true as well (`sets` not
being an array, say), the case is built on the smallest IR that
isolates it -- see `mini` below -- so the named rule is the only one
the document breaks.
`loc` is the path INSIDE the ir. The router prefixes `body`, `ir`
before it reaches a client (Ruling 30: consumers key on `loc`).
Cases whose rule is `where: domain` in the contract can only be
judged against real rows; the client marks them skipped and counts
them, so a rule silently moving from `shape` to `domain` fails there.
Four cases carry `generate` instead of `ir`: an IR big enough to
break a limit is not worth 500 hand-written lines. Both harnesses
build it from the spec -- `nestedAdd`, `wideAdd`, `padNote` and
`padNoteWide` are the only four forms, and each is a line or two on
each side. `padNoteWide` exists because ASCII padding cannot tell a
byte count from a character count, and the two languages have to
agree which side of the limit a document falls on.
`domain` describes the world the server builds to judge the `domain`
rules. It is the Workforce demo's shape (app/seed.py) minus its
entities, which is what lets `workforce` below be asserted equal to
the seeded IR itself.

valid.name: mini
valid.why: The smallest model the contract admits: one scalar binary variable, no constraints, no objective. It is the base the structural invalid cases are built on, so it has to be valid or those cases would be wrong in two ways.

valid.name: declared_set_need_not_be_used
valid.why: `unit` is in `sets` and in no expression. `sets` says what the dataset must freeze, not what the arithmetic touches, so this is legal -- and it is what the seeded model does.

valid.name: soft_constraint
valid.why: `severity: soft` with a positive integer weight -- the shape `scenario.patch`'s `soften` produces and `harden` reverses.

valid.name: filtered_sum
valid.why: A `where` on a binding, using the expression catalogue's own `=` over a boolean attribute of the bound set: weekend days only.

valid.name: enum_filter_with_a_list_operator
valid.why: `in` over an enum, with a list value -- the one filter operator whose value is an array. `operatorsByType` in the expression catalogue is what says an enum offers it.

valid.name: integer_variable_with_bounds
valid.why: The other admitted variable domain. Bounds are optional and, when given, are integers -- like every other number in a v1 model.

valid.name: weighted_objective_with_two_terms
valid.why: Two terms, two ids, two weights, one sense -- and `add` used inside one of them.

valid.name: continuous_variable
valid.why: a continuous variable, admitted by migration 0015. It is what makes LP a class the platform can express, and what gives the solver-selection policy something to choose between

valid.name: number_attribute_as_coefficient
valid.why: `hourly_rate` is a `number`, and reading it as a coefficient is exactly how a model becomes continuous. It is admitted since migration 0015 and the classifier reports `fractional-data`, which routes it away from cp-sat

valid.name: staffing_across_a_hierarchy
valid.why: The question the traversal decision note says a planner asks first and v1 could not express: staffing for a unit counting everything beneath it. Two walks compose -- `reports_to` at `any_or_self` depth gathers the sub-units, then `works_in` gathers the people in each -- which is the case option 2 of that note (closures only) could not have answered

valid.name: one_hop_traversal_with_a_filter
valid.why: The simplest walk there is -- one edge, no closure -- and it composes with `where`, which is the property that makes `via` a binding form rather than a term kind

valid.name: quadratic_objective

valid.name: quadratic_rule

valid.name: volume_discount_pwl
valid.why: A piecewise-linear cost (version 2): 5 a unit for the first two, 3 for the next two, 2 after -- a price-break curve, which is concave and needs the curve itself, not its tangents.

valid.name: diminishing_returns_fn
valid.why: Functions from the catalogue (version 2): ten to spend between two uses, one returning log(1 + x) and the other sqrt(y) -- both concave, so each extra unit returns less.

valid.name: shift_blocks_scheduled
valid.why: Scheduling (version 2): an interval ties a start and an end variable, `end = start + size`, and may be absent when its presence is 0. `no_overlap` keeps one day's blocks apart; `cumulative` lets at most two run at once.

valid.name: demand_uncertain_within_a_range
valid.why: A parameter may say how its values may be wrong (version 2): each within 10% of itself, at most two of a rule's cells at once -- what a robust solve reads.

invalid.why: an array is not a model
the document carries its version from the first one ever written

JSON true is not version 1, but in Python `True == 1` and `bool` subclasses `int`, so a validator that compared with == alone would accept this and the two languages would disagree about the same document
a version this platform does not express is refused, not guessed at (it reads 1 and 2)
a frozen model states its constraints, even when it has none
a top-level typo (here `sense` outside `objective`) is a silently ignored model half
snapshot_dataset() reads `sets` with jsonb_array_elements_text; an object reaches it as SQLSTATE 22023, i.e. a 500
entity_type.name carries the same CHECK; a name that cannot satisfy it cannot name a real type
a repeated set would be frozen twice into the same key
snapshot_dataset() reads it with jsonb_object_keys
parameter_def.name carries the same CHECK
the declaration carries the index; an array here loses it
a parameter is indexed by an ordered, non-empty list of sets, as parameter_def.index_type_ids is
a parameter indexed by a set the model never declares is indexed by data the dataset will not carry
variables are keyed by name, like parameters
a model with nothing to decide is not a model
variable names are used verbatim in solution keys, so they follow the platform's one name rule
the declaration carries the index and the domain
a scalar variable declares an empty index, never a missing or scalar one
a variable indexed by an undeclared set would be sized from data the dataset does not carry
nothing may default a variable's domain: it decides the model's class
'real' is a plausible mistake for 'continuous', which is the point: the vocabulary is closed, and a domain outside it is named in the refusal rather than silently treated as one of the three
and on a bound
an inverted bound makes a variable with no admissible value, which is an infeasibility nobody wrote down on purpose
constraints are ordered and addressed by id, not keyed
a bare id is the shape the seeded sketch nearly had
`kind` is a Phase 1 column, not a v1 IR key; accepting it would store a field nothing reads
constraint ids travel into scenario.patch and constraint_result.constraint_id; one spelling rule for all three
constraint_result is keyed (run_id, constraint_id); two constraints with one id could not both report

invalid.why: strict inequalities are not in v1: over integers they are the non-strict one shifted by 1, and admitting both spellings would make two IRs for one model
constraint_result.hard is a boolean; there is no third state to record
and on a penalty, where `true` would become a weight of 1 -- the lightest possible penalty, chosen by a type error rather than by anyone

the other half of the same rule, which no other case reached: a HARD constraint carrying a weight. A weight there is a penalty for breaking something that cannot be broken -- the author meant `soft`, or meant a scenario
a soft constraint with no penalty is a constraint the solver is free to ignore, which is a disable nobody asked for
a binding names an index AND the set it ranges over; a bare string says only half
index names are the one vocabulary a term may invent, so they follow the same rule as every other name here
shadowing would make `d` mean whichever binding the reader looked at last
ranging over a set the model never declared is ranging over data the dataset will not carry
an empty `forall` is a constraint written as if it were indexed and is not; omitting the key says that unambiguously
filters are an AND-list; v1 has no groups and no `or`
every filter states all three of attribute, comparison and value; v1 has no unary filters
the filter vocabulary is a subset of the expression catalogue's operators, and nothing outside it
a bare number is not a term: every term says what kind it is, so a reader never has to infer
an unknown kind is a term this version cannot compile, and guessing at it is how a solver silently drops half a model
two kinds in one object leaves which one wins to the reader's key order
the `bool` trap on a coefficient: `isinstance(True, int)` is true in Python, so a coefficient of `true` would become a silent 1
a number written as a string. 1.5 is a legitimate coefficient since migration 0015; "1.5" is a client with a type bug, and accepting it would make the contract's one numeric type two
the same fault one level down, INSIDE a sum's body. Without this case a validator that bound a sum's indices and then never walked what it was summing would pass every other fixture in this file
a misspelt variable is the commonest way an IR compiles to a smaller model than it reads as
a variable subscripted with fewer indices than it was declared with is a different variable
a free index has no range, so the constraint has no instances
`open` is indexed [day, shift]; subscripting it [s, d] type-checks by arity and is the wrong model
a sum with no `over` is not a sum; it is its own body with a misleading name
an empty sum of terms is zero, and writing zero as `{"const": 0}` says so
exactly two factors, so the linearity rule below is a check on a pair and not a search
x*(x*y) in a rule is cubic. A rule may be quadratic -- two variables at most -- and no higher, the same ceiling as a weighted objective
the key is omitted for a feasibility problem; it is never a bare sense
`run.objective` records one number; there is no third direction to record it in
Pareto is a frontier of answers, not a mode of one number; lex is the other ordering this version expresses
an objective with no terms is no objective, and omitting the key says that
and on an objective term's weight
THE SEEDED SKETCH'S OTHER FAULT: `{"id": "o_cost", "weight": 1}` names a term that nothing defines
a number written as a string. 1.5 is a legitimate coefficient since migration 0015; "1.5" is a client with a type bug, and accepting it would make the contract's one numeric type two
term ids are how a result explains which part of the objective cost what

a term nested past the limit is past what a builder can render and what a reader can check. `nestedAdd` wraps a `const` in 14 `add`s; the outermost is at depth 1, so the thirteenth is the first past maxDepth 12 and the loc names it

the bound on total work, so an IR cannot be a denial of service against the validator. The counter increments on entry to each term and the refusal names the term that took it past the limit: the `add` is term 1, so term 501 is summand 499

the same limit with MULTI-BYTE padding. `padNoteWide` is 200000 two-byte characters: under the limit counted in characters (or in JavaScript string length), over it counted in UTF-8 bytes. Without this case both validators could measure whichever they liked and still agree with the ASCII case above
the transport bound. Checked first, before any other rule, because everything else walks the document
TODAY THIS IS A 500: snapshot_dataset() raises `IR set "%" has no entity_type in this domain`, as P0001, long after the version was accepted. It belongs at submit time
the same 500, by the other loop of the same function

demand is declared over [day, shift] in the domain. An IR that reads it as [shift, day] snapshots without complaint and solves the wrong model -- snapshot_dataset() emits cells keyed by type name, so nothing downstream notices either
the attribute travels in the snapshot's set rows; one the entity type does not declare is never in them
`hired_on` is a date. `number` became arithmetic with migration 0015, but a date has no meaning as a coefficient and never will
`operatorsByType` in the expression catalogue gives a boolean only `=` and `!=`, and this reads the same table rather than a second one
1 is not a boolean. `entity_validate` would not store it in that attribute, so no row can ever match
one name is not a list of them. `snapshot_dataset()` reads this with jsonb_array_elements_text, exactly as it reads `sets`
`relationship_type.name` carries the same CHECK every other name on this platform does, and it is capitalised here
declaring the same edge type twice would freeze it twice under one key; `sets` refuses the same thing for the same reason
the relationship name alone does not say which end the walk starts from, and there is no default that would not be a guess
`reports_to` is never declared, so `snapshot_dataset()` would not freeze its edges and the walk would read data the frozen document does not carry
naming both ends says the walk starts at both of them; the end named is where the anchor sits, so exactly one of them can be
the walk starts at an index nothing bound. A free anchor has no entity to walk from, which is the traversal form of the rule that every index is bound
`all` is not one of the three depths; the vocabulary is closed so that a document cannot ask for a walk the compiler has no expansion for
a well-formed name for a relationship type this domain does not have. Only the domain's rows can say so, which is why this is the traversal twin of `set_not_in_domain`
`works_in` runs employee to unit, so its `from` end is an employee; anchoring a unit there walks the edge backwards. The document cannot see this -- only the relationship type's own endpoint rows can
walking `works_in` twice would step from a unit to an employee and then look for an edge out of a unit again. Only a relationship whose two ends are the same entity type composes with itself
x*(y*z) is cubic. Counting factors that mention a variable sees two here and would pass it; only the degree catches it, which is why the check counts degree

a lexicographic objective holds each term at its best before the next; holding a quadratic term would turn every later stage into a quadratic rule, so the contract keeps a lexicographic objective linear and only a weighted one may be quadratic
`when` is a version 2 construct; a version 1 document that uses it is not a version 1 document; its one when is the only thing wrong with it
a when names its variable's index, even an empty one, as every variable reference does
a rule is switched by a yes-or-no decision; `ship_b` is a quantity
a rule that may be broken at a cost is not also switched off
a conditional rule is linear: indicator constraints take a linear rule
a piecewise-linear term is a version 2 construct
one point is a value, not a curve: a pwl needs at least two
x must increase, or one x would have two values
a function term is a version 2 construct
tan is not in the catalogue
a function with nothing to apply it to
exp(x * y): the argument multiplies two decisions
an interval is version 2
an interval's window is its start's and end's bounds, not its own
a start is an integer variable, not a yes-or-no
a size is never negative
an interval is not a number; its end variable is
a scheduling rule is version 2
a constraint is one expression or one scheduling rule, not both
no_overlap is over intervals, not start times
a scheduling rule has no price for being broken
a demand is data, not a decision
an uncertainty is version 2
